title: Solve a positive-definite system by Cholesky factorization
aliases: triangular solves for symmetric positive definite matrix
pattern: For real symmetric positive-definite A, write A=LLᵀ with L lower triangular and positive diagonal. Solve Ly=b and then Lᵀx=y.
applies: A is real, symmetric, and positive definite.
The factor can be reused when the same A has several right-hand sides.
steps: Work down each column j. Set L[j,j]=sqrt(A[j,j]−Σ_{k<j} L[j,k]²).
For i>j, set L[i,j]=(A[i,j]−Σ_{k<j} L[i,k]L[j,k])/L[j,j].
Use forward substitution on Ly=b, then back substitution on Lᵀx=y.
pitfalls: A nonpositive radicand in exact arithmetic signals that the positive-definite assumptions or arithmetic failed.
Solving with L in both substitutions changes the system.
checks: Multiply LLᵀ and compare it with A.
Check the residual b−Ax directly.

example.answer: The positive-diagonal factor is L=[[2,0],[1,2]]. Forward substitution gives y=(4,4)ᵀ. Back substitution gives x=(1,2)ᵀ, whose product with A is (8,12)ᵀ.

title: Bound right-hand-side error using a matrix condition number
aliases: relative error in a linear system
pattern: For nonsingular A and nonzero b, κ∞(A)=||A||∞||A⁻¹||∞, where ||M||∞ is the maximum absolute row sum. With A fixed, ||Δx||∞/||x||∞ ≤ κ∞(A)||Δb||∞/||b||∞.
applies: The right-hand side b changes while the same nonsingular matrix A defines both solutions.
Use the same induced norm for the matrix and both vector errors.
steps: Find the maximum absolute row sums of A and A⁻¹ and multiply them.
Divide the maximum component of |Δb| by the maximum component of |b|.
Multiply by κ∞ for a worst-case bound. When the actual perturbation is known, solve AΔx=Δb to measure its effect.
pitfalls: Using the largest single matrix entry in place of an absolute row sum gives a different norm.
A worst-case bound can be much larger than the error for a particular direction.
checks: For a nonsingular matrix κ∞ is at least 1.
Check that AΔx=Δb and compare its measured relative size with the bound.

example.problem: For A=[[2,1],[1,2]], b=(3,3)ᵀ, and Δb=(0.03,−0.03)ᵀ, compute κ∞ and the actual relative infinity-norm change in x.
example.answer: The row sums of A are 3 and those of A⁻¹=(1/3)[[2,−1],[−1,2]] are 1, so κ∞=3. Initially x=(1,1)ᵀ. The perturbation direction has eigenvalue 1, so Δx=Δb. The relative change is 0.03, exactly 3 times the relative input change 0.01.

title: Find a power-series solution at an ordinary point
pattern: For a linear ODE with analytic normalized coefficients near x₀, substitute y=Σaₙ(x−x₀)ⁿ, shift every series to matching powers, and equate coefficients.
applies: The highest-derivative coefficient is nonzero at x₀ and the normalized coefficients are analytic there.
Initial values at x₀ determine the first coefficients.
steps: Set a₀=y(x₀), a₁=y′(x₀), and any higher initial coefficients using derivatives divided by factorials.
Differentiate term by term and shift indices before multiplying by the known coefficient series.
Equate the coefficient of each power to derive a recurrence. Compute enough terms to reach the requested degree.
pitfalls: An index shift can leave a special low-power equation, such as the constant term.
Using ordinary-point series at a singular point can omit essential solution branches.
checks: Verify the first terms of the residual by substitution.
Substitute x=x₀ into the series and its derivatives to check the initial values.

example.problem: Find the terms through x⁶ of y″+xy=0 with y(0)=1 and y′(0)=0.
example.answer: For xⁿ the equation is (n+2)(n+1)aₙ₊₂+aₙ₋₁=0 with a₋₁=0. Starting from a₀=1 and a₁=0 gives a₂=0, a₃=−1/6, a₄=a₅=0, and a₆=1/180. The requested terms are 1−x³/6+x⁶/180.

title: Use the Frobenius indicial equation at a regular singular point
pattern: For x²y″+xp(x)y′+q(x)y=0 with p and q analytic at 0, insert y=xʳΣaₙxⁿ on x>0. The coefficient of xʳ gives r(r−1)+p(0)r+q(0)=0.
applies: After rewriting the second-order linear homogeneous ODE, p and q are analytic at the singular point.
A noninteger power uses a fixed side of the singular point, here x>0.
steps: Shift the regular singular point to zero and write the normalized equation.
Derive the indicial polynomial from the lowest power with a₀≠0.
For each root, match higher powers to find the recurrence. Repeated roots or roots with integer difference require checking whether the second branch needs a logarithm.
pitfalls: A zero denominator in the recurrence may require a second-solution analysis.
Taking a₀=0 before deriving the indicial polynomial changes the leading exponent.
checks: Verify the lowest-power cancellation and at least two recurrence coefficients.
If the roots differ by a noninteger, check that the two branches have distinct leading powers.

example.problem: Find the first three coefficients of both Frobenius branches of 2xy″+y′−y=0 for x>0.
example.answer: Multiplying by x/2 gives indicial roots 0 and 1/2. For n≥1, aₙ=aₙ₋₁/[2(n+r)(n+r−1/2)]. With a₀=1 the branches start 1+x+x²/6 and x^(1/2)(1+x/3+x²/30), respectively.

title: Find an order-statistic CDF by counting observations below a threshold
pattern: For an iid sample with CDF F, P(X₍ₖ₎≤t)=P(Binomial(n,F(t))≥k) because at least k observations must be at or below t.
applies: The n observations are independent and identically distributed.
X₍ₖ₎ denotes the kth smallest observation. A density calculation also requires differentiability where used.
steps: Compute the chance F(t) for one observation to be at or below t.
Sum the binomial probabilities for counts k through n.
Complement the CDF for a strict upper-tail probability. Differentiate within the support if a density is requested and exists.
pitfalls: For kth largest, convert the index to n−k+1 before using the rule.
A density alone can miss point masses when the original distribution has atoms.
checks: At k=1 the CDF reduces to 1−(1−F(t))ⁿ.
At k=n it reduces to F(t)ⁿ.

example.problem: Draw four iid Uniform(0,1) values. Find the CDF of the third smallest and P(X₍₃₎>1/2).
example.answer: On 0≤t≤1, the CDF is 4t³(1−t)+t⁴=4t³−3t⁴. It is 0 below 0 and 1 above 1. Evaluating and complementing at t=1/2 gives 1−5/16=11/16.

title: Find Galton–Watson extinction from the offspring generating function
pattern: For one founder with offspring generating function G(s), the eventual extinction probability is the smallest fixed point of G on [0,1]. For m independent founders it is qᵐ.
applies: Every individual has the same offspring distribution and offspring counts are independent.
Zero is absorbing and the question asks whether some finite generation becomes empty.
steps: Construct G(s)=Σpₖsᵏ for the offspring count.
Set q₀=0 and qₙ₊₁=G(qₙ) for extinction by generation n+1.
Solve G(s)=s and choose the smallest root in [0,1]. Monotonicity from q₀=0 keeps every iterate below each fixed point.
pitfalls: The root 1 is always present and can fail to be the smallest root.
The power qᵐ depends on independence of the founder lineages.
checks: Check the chosen root by substitution and confirm it is a probability.
Check finite-generation iterates from 0 against the claimed smallest root.

example.problem: An individual has zero offspring with probability 1/4 and two with probability 3/4. Find eventual extinction probabilities for one and two independent founders.
example.answer: G(s)=1/4+3s²/4. Solving 3s²−4s+1=0 gives 1/3 and 1. The smaller root is 1/3, so extinction from two founders has probability (1/3)²=1/9.

title: Use a t interval or test for a simple regression slope
pattern: With an intercept and Sxx=Σ(xᵢ−x̄)²>0, SE(b)=sqrt(SSE/((n−2)Sxx)). For H₀ slope=β₀ use t=(b−β₀)/SE(b) with n−2 degrees of freedom.
applies: Conditional on the predictor values, the simple linear mean model has independent normal errors with common variance for exact finite-sample t inference.
There are more than two observations, variation in x, and a positive residual variance estimate.
steps: Fit the line and compute SSE from its vertical residuals.
Use SSE/(n−2) to estimate the error variance, then divide by Sxx and take the square root for the slope standard error.
Use the chosen t quantile for the confidence interval or test the null slope with the corresponding t tail.
pitfalls: Using n−1 degrees of freedom overlooks that both intercept and slope were fitted.
Heteroskedastic or dependent residuals require a different uncertainty calculation.
checks: For a two-sided test, a null slope outside the corresponding interval is rejected at the matching level.
Check units of the slope and its standard error.

example.problem: Under the normal-error simple regression model, find a 95% confidence interval for the slope from (−2,0), (−1,0), (1,4), and (2,8).
example.answer: The fitted line is ŷ=3+2x. Its residuals (1,−1,−1,1) give SSE=4, and Sxx=10. The slope standard error is 1/√5 with two degrees of freedom. The interval is 2±t(0.975,2)/√5, approximately [0.076,3.924].

title: Compute a one-sided Fisher exact test for a 2×2 table
pattern: Condition on the row and column totals. With N observations, M total successes, and n in group A, P(X=k)=C(M,k)C(N−M,n−k)/C(N,n) under the null.
applies: The 2×2 table contains independent observations with equal success probabilities under the null, or a randomized allocation with exchangeable group labels under the null.
The one-sided alternative is a larger success proportion in group A.
steps: Fix both row totals and both column totals. Let X count successes in group A.
Find the feasible integer range max(0,n−(N−M)) through min(n,M).
Sum the exact conditional probabilities for X at least as large as the observed value.
pitfalls: Changing which group or outcome is called a success can reverse the tail.
Doubling a one-sided value can differ from a two-sided exact test, which needs its own definition.
checks: Each table in the sum must keep all four margins fixed.
A p-value must lie between 0 and 1 and includes the observed table.

example.problem: Group A has three successes and one failure. Group B has zero successes and four failures. Find the one-sided exact p-value for higher success in A.
example.answer: N=8, M=3, and n=4. The observed X=3 is its largest feasible value, so the tail is C(3,3)C(5,1)/C(8,4)=5/70=1/14.

title: Find a shortest weighted path with Dijkstra's algorithm
pattern: Keep tentative distances, repeatedly settle the unsettled vertex of minimum distance, and relax each outgoing edge u→v with d(v)=min(d(v),d(u)+w(u,v)).
applies: The directed or undirected graph has nonnegative edge weights.
The problem asks for distances or paths from one start vertex.
steps: Give the start distance 0 and every other vertex infinity.
Extract the smallest current tentative distance. Skip stale queue entries if updates create duplicates.
Record a predecessor whenever relaxation improves a distance. Stop at the target when it is settled and reconstruct the path from its predecessors.
pitfalls: Stopping when a target is first discovered can leave a shorter path unexplored.
A negative edge can invalidate the settling argument.
checks: Add the reconstructed path weights and compare them with the settled distance.
Every outgoing edge from a vertex settled before the target has been considered for relaxation.

example.problem: Find a shortest path from A to E in the undirected graph with edges AB=4, AC=1, CB=2, CD=6, BD=1, DE=3, and CE=10.
example.answer: Settling gives distances A=0, C=1, B=3, D=4, E=7. The predecessors reconstruct A→C→B→D→E, with total 1+2+1+3=7.

title: Increase a bipartite matching using an augmenting path
pattern: An augmenting path starts and ends at unmatched vertices and alternates between unused and matched edges. Flipping all its edges increases matching size by one.
applies: A finite bipartite graph has a current unweighted matching.
The goal is to construct a larger or maximum-cardinality matching.
steps: Start a search at all unmatched left vertices. Traverse unused edges left to right and matched edges right to left.
When the search reaches an unmatched right vertex, reconstruct that alternating path and flip membership of every path edge.
Repeat until no augmenting path exists. The augmenting-path criterion then certifies maximum cardinality.
pitfalls: Starting or ending at a matched vertex can preserve size or violate matching constraints.
A matching that cannot accept a single new edge can still be increased by a longer path.
checks: After a flip, each vertex is incident to at most one matched edge.
The path has one more previously unused edge than matched edge.

example.problem: Left vertices a, b, c have neighbor sets {X,Z}, {X,Y}, {Y}. The current matching is a–X and b–Y. Find an augmenting path and a larger matching.
example.answer: Use c→Y→b→X→a→Z. The unused edges c–Y, b–X, a–Z become matched and the other two become unused. The resulting matching has size three.

title: Interpolate values and endpoint slopes with a cubic Hermite polynomial
pattern: Set h=b−a, t=(x−a)/h. Then p=(2t³−3t²+1)yₐ+(t³−2t²+t)h mₐ+(−2t³+3t²)yᵦ+(t³−t²)h mᵦ.
applies: The two nodes a<b are distinct. Both function values y and derivatives m with respect to x are known.
steps: Normalize x to t so that the endpoints become 0 and 1.
Evaluate the four Hermite basis polynomials, scaling each derivative datum by h.
Combine the terms and expand in x if a standard polynomial is required.
pitfalls: Omitting h from the derivative terms gives the wrong x-slopes when h differs from 1.
Endpoint data determine the cubic interpolant. Error away from the endpoints depends on the underlying function.
checks: Substitute a and b to check the values.
Differentiate with respect to x using dt/dx=1/h and check both slopes.

example.problem: Find the cubic with p(0)=1, p′(0)=1, p(2)=5, and p′(2)=0. Evaluate p(1).
example.answer: Here h=2 and t=x/2. Substitution gives p(x)=1+x+2x²−3x³/4. Both endpoint derivatives match and p(1)=13/4.

title: Integrate with two-point Gauss–Legendre quadrature
pattern: With m=(a+b)/2 and h=(b−a)/2, use ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx ≈ h[f(m−h/√3)+f(m+h/√3)]. The rule is exact for polynomials of degree at most 3.
applies: The interval [a,b] is finite and both interior function values are defined.
For accuracy beyond cubic exactness, the integrand is sufficiently smooth for the intended approximation.
steps: Map the two nodes ±1/√3 on [−1,1] to m±h/√3.
Evaluate the integrand at the mapped nodes and multiply their sum by h.
For a nonpolynomial integrand, use subdivision or an independent error estimate when precision matters.
pitfalls: Dropping the factor h ignores the change of variables.
A discontinuity or endpoint singularity can make the two-node estimate unreliable.
checks: On a constant integrand the result is the interval length times that constant.
Cubic exactness follows by checking powers 0, 1, 2, and 3 on [−1,1].

example.problem: Apply the two-point Gauss–Legendre rule to ∫₀² (x³+2x²+1) dx.
example.answer: The nodes are 1±1/√3 with weights 1. The x³ terms sum to 4, the 2x² terms to 16/3, and the constants to 2. The exact integral is 34/3.
